questiontext.text: What is a Count-Min Sketch primarily used for?

answer.text: Estimating item frequencies (counts) in a data stream using sublinear space

feedback.text: Correct — it approximates how often each item appears while using very little memory.

answer.text: Testing whether an item is a member of a set

feedback.text: That is a Bloom filter; a Count-Min Sketch estimates counts, not mere membership.

answer.text: Keeping items sorted for ordered traversal

feedback.text: No — it stores counters, not ordered keys.

answer.text: Sorting a stream in O(n) time

feedback.text: No — it does not sort; it summarizes frequencies.

generalfeedback.text: A Count-Min Sketch is a probabilistic sketch that estimates the frequency of items in a stream using far less space than an exact counter table.

questiontext.text: What is the internal structure of a Count-Min Sketch?

answer.text: A 2D array of counters with width w and depth d, plus d hash functions (one per row)

feedback.text: Correct — each of the d hashes maps an item to one counter in its row.

answer.text: A single bit array with k hash functions

feedback.text: That describes a Bloom filter, which uses single bits, not counters.

answer.text: A multi-level linked list with random node heights

feedback.text: That describes a skip list, not a Count-Min Sketch.

answer.text: A balanced search tree keyed by item value

feedback.text: No — a Count-Min Sketch uses hashed counter arrays, not a tree.

generalfeedback.text: A Count-Min Sketch is a d-by-w table of integer counters; each row has its own hash function mapping items into that row's w counters.

questiontext.text: How does a Count-Min Sketch estimate an item's count at query time?

answer.text: It reads the d counters the item hashes to and returns their minimum

feedback.text: Correct — taking the minimum discards the rows most inflated by collisions.

answer.text: It returns the sum of the d hashed counters

feedback.text: No — summing would grossly overcount; the minimum is used.

answer.text: It returns the average of all counters in the table

feedback.text: No — only the d counters for that specific item are consulted, and via their minimum.

answer.text: It performs a binary search over the counters

feedback.text: No — counters are addressed directly by hashing; there is no search.

generalfeedback.text: An update adds to one counter per row; a query takes the minimum of the item's d counters, since that value is least affected by collisions.

questiontext.text: What controls the accuracy (error) of a Count-Min Sketch estimate?

answer.text: The width w bounds the error magnitude and the depth d bounds the failure probability

feedback.text: Correct — wider rows reduce collision error; more rows make a bad estimate less likely.

answer.text: The specific values of the items counted

feedback.text: No — accuracy is governed by the dimensions w and d, not item values.

answer.text: Whether the counters are kept in sorted order

feedback.text: No — counters are addressed by hashing and have no order.

answer.text: The recursion depth of the update procedure

feedback.text: No — updates are O(d) and not recursive.

generalfeedback.text: Larger width w tightens the additive error (proportional to e/w of the stream size) and larger depth d exponentially reduces the chance of exceeding that error.

questiontext.text: A Count-Min Sketch may overestimate an item's true count but never underestimates it.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — collisions can only add to counters, so the reported count is always ≥ the true count.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — because counters only accumulate, the estimate can never fall below the true count.

questiontext.text: A Count-Min Sketch uses sublinear space: much less than storing an exact counter for every distinct item.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the fixed w-by-d table stays small even as the number of distinct items grows.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — the whole point is a compact fixed-size table rather than one counter per item.

questiontext.text: Because hash collisions only add to counters, a Count-Min Sketch can only ______ an item's true count (fill the verb, English).

answer.text: overestimate

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: overestimate*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: overcount

feedback.text: Correct — it can only overcount (overestimate).

answer.text: over-estimate

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a Count-Min Sketch are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is well suited to finding heavy hitters in a data stream

feedback.text: Yes — approximate high-frequency items are its classic application.

answer.text: Its estimates are biased upward (never below the true count)

feedback.text: Yes — collisions only add, so it overestimates, never underestimates.

answer.text: It stores each distinct key explicitly to allow exact counts

feedback.text: No — it keeps only hashed counters, giving approximate counts.

answer.text: It can underestimate counts when the table gets crowded

feedback.text: No — it never underestimates; crowding only increases overestimation.

generalfeedback.text: A Count-Min Sketch summarizes stream frequencies in sublinear space; it overestimates (never underestimates), stores no explicit keys, and is ideal for heavy-hitter detection.
